<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:even-paths-intro}
For all integers $r_1,\ldots,r_k\ge1$,
$$
 f(P_{2r_1}\square\cdots\square P_{2r_k})
 =\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil.
$$
In particular,
$f(P_{2r}^{\square k})=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$ 
for $r,k\ge 1$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:trees-intro}
If $T_1,\ldots,T_k$ are trees with perfect matchings, then
$$
 f(T_1\square\cdots\square T_k)=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil.
$$
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:all-path-intro}
Let $n_1,\ldots,n_k\ge 2$ be integers, let
$G=P_{n_1}\square\cdots\square P_{n_k}$,
and let $e$ be the number of even integers among $n_1,\ldots,n_k$.  Then
$$
 f(G)=
 \begin{cases}
  \lceil\sqrt e\rceil, & e\ge1,\\
  2, & e=0\text{ and }n_1=\cdots=n_k=3,\\
  1, & e=0\text{ and at least one }n_i\ge5.
 \end{cases}
$$
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:fixed-excess-intro}
Let $k\ge1$, let $T_1,\ldots,T_k$ be trees with perfect matchings, and put $D=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$. 
\begin{enumerate}
 \item[$(i)$] If $1\le t\le 2^{D-\lceil\log_2D\rceil-1}$, then $f_t(T_1\square\cdots\square T_k)=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$.
 \item[$(ii)$] If $k\ge2$ and at least one $T_i$ is not $K_2$, then $f_2(T_1\square\cdots\square T_k)=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:parity-twist-excess}
Let $n\ge1$ and let $F:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$. Define
$\chi_F(x)=(-1)^{|x|+F(x)}$. Then
$$
 d_{\chi_F}(x)=s(F,x)\quad\text{for every }x,
 \quad \sum_x\chi_F(x)=-2A(F).
$$
Consequently, one color class has $2^{n-1}+|A(F)|$ vertices and induces a subgraph of maximum degree at most $s(F)$. If $A(F)\ne0$, then
$f_{|A(F)|}(Q_n)\le s(F)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Across a cube edge the parity of $|x|$ changes. The endpoints therefore
receive the same $\chi_F$-color exactly when $F$ changes value across the
edge, proving the degree assertion. Since $(-1)^{F(x)}=1-2F(x)$ and the
parity character has sum zero,
$$
 \sum_x\chi_F(x)
 =\sum_x(-1)^{|x|}\bigl(1-2F(x)\bigr)=-2A(F).
$$
The two color classes thus differ in size by $2|A(F)|$, proving the
remaining assertions.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:cube-coloring}
For every $k\ge1$, there is a function
$\chi:\{0,1\}^k\to\{-1,1\}$ such that
$$
 \sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}\chi(x)=2
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 d_\chi(x)\le\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil
 \quad\text{for every }x.
$$
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Put $D=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$ and
$q=\lceil k/D\rceil$.  Then $q\le D$.  Partition $[k]$ into nonempty sets
$I_1,\ldots,I_q$, each of size at most $D$, and define
$$
 F(x)=\prod_{j=1}^q
 \left(1-\prod_{i\in I_j}(1-x_i)\right),
 \quad x\in\{0,1\}^k.
$$
Thus $F(x)=1$ exactly when every block $I_j$ contains a coordinate equal to $1$.

If $F(x)=0$, flipping a coordinate can change $F(x)$ only when exactly one block is all zero; that block has at most $D$ coordinates. If $F(x)=1$, a sensitive coordinate must be the unique $1$ in its block, so there are at most $q$ such coordinates. Hence, $s(F)\le \max\{D,q\}=D$.

Since $F$ is the conjunction of the OR functions on the disjoint blocks,
$$
 A(F)=\prod_{j=1}^q A(\operatorname{OR}_{|I_j|})=(-1)^q.
$$
Set $\chi=(-1)^{q+1}\chi_F$. Lemma~\ref{lem:parity-twist-excess} gives
$$
 \sum_x\chi(x)=(-1)^{q+1}(-2A(F))=2,
 \quad d_\chi(x)=s(F,x)\le D.
$$
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:huang}
If $U\subseteq V(Q_k)$ and $|U|\ge 2^{k-1}+1$, then
$$
 \Delta(Q_k[U])\ge\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil.
$$
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:cube-cell-bound}
Let $k\ge1$ and $\ell\ge0$. Let $G_1,\ldots,G_k$ be bipartite graphs with perfect matchings,
and let $H_1,\ldots,H_\ell$ be bipartite graphs. Assume that every
factor has at least one vertex.
Put
$$
 G=G_1\square\cdots\square G_k
   \square H_1\square\cdots\square H_\ell,
 \quad N=|V(G)|.
$$
Then $\alpha(G)=N/2$, and
$$
 f_t(G)\ge\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil
 \quad\text{for }1\le t\le N/2.
$$
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Replicating a perfect matching of $G_1$ over all choices of the other
coordinates gives a perfect matching of $G$. An independent set contains
at most one endpoint of each matching edge, so $\alpha(G)\le N/2$.
Since $G$ is bipartite, the reverse inequality also holds.

Fix a perfect matching in each $G_i$. Products of their edges, together
with a fixed vertex in each $H_j$, partition $V(G)$ into induced copies
of $Q_k$. Every set $U$ with $|U|=N/2+t>N/2$ contains more than half the
vertices of at least one such copy. Theorem~\ref{thm:huang} therefore gives
$\Delta(G[U])\ge\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:bridge-gate}
Let $G$ be a connected bipartite graph with a perfect matching $M$, and let
$uv\in M$ be a bridge. There are functions
$$
 \tau:V(G)\to\{0,1\},\quad
 \eta:V(G)\to\{-1,1\}
$$
with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item[$(i)$] $\sum_{\tau(x)=0}\eta(x)=\sum_{\tau(x)=1}\eta(x)=1$;
 \item[$(ii)$] for every edge $xy\in E(G)\setminus\{uv\}$,
 $\tau(x)=\tau(y)$ and $\eta(x)=-\eta(y)$;
 \item[$(iii)$] $\eta(u)=\eta(v)$ and $\tau(u)\ne\tau(v)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $L$ and $R$ be the components of $G-uv$ containing $u$ and $v$, respectively.  Reverse $\rho$ if necessary so that $\rho(u)=1$ and $\rho(v)=-1$.  The matching $M-uv$ pairs all vertices of $L$ except $u$ and all vertices of $R$ except $v$. Since the endpoints of each matching edge have opposite $\rho$-values,
$$
 \sum_{x\in L}\rho(x)=1,
 \quad
 \sum_{x\in R}\rho(x)=-1.
$$
Set $\tau=0$ on $L$, $\tau=1$ on $R$, and
$\eta(x)=(-1)^{\tau(x)}\rho(x)$.
Then $\sum_{x\in L}\eta(x)=\sum_{x\in R}\eta(x)=1$ and $\eta(u)=\eta(v)=1$.  Inside either component, $\tau$ is
constant and $\eta$ changes across every edge, whereas both $\rho$ and $\tau$ change across $uv$.  This proves all three assertions.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:general-product}
Let $G_1,\ldots,G_k$ be connected bipartite graphs, each having a perfect matching that contains a bridge.  Let $H_1,\ldots,H_\ell$ be unbalanced
bipartite graphs, where $\ell\ge 0$, and put
$$
 G=G_1\square\cdots\square G_k
   \square H_1\square\cdots\square H_\ell.
$$
If $k\ge 1$, then
$f(G)=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $N=|V(G)|$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cube-cell-bound},
$\alpha(G)=N/2$ and $f(G)\ge\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$.

For the upper bound, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:bridge-gate} to each $G_i$, and
write the resulting functions as $\tau_i$ and $\eta_i$.  For every $H_j$,
choose a bipartition character $\zeta_j$ with positive sum; this is possible
because $H_j$ is unbalanced.  Take the cube coloring $\chi$ from
Lemma~\ref{lem:cube-coloring} and for each $v=(x_1,\ldots,x_k,y_1,\ldots,y_\ell)\in V(G)$ define
$$
 \Psi(v)=\Psi(x_1,\ldots,x_k,y_1,\ldots,y_\ell)
  = \chi(\tau_1(x_1),\ldots,\tau_k(x_k))
    \cdot\prod_{i=1}^k\eta_i(x_i)
    \prod_{j=1}^\ell\zeta_j(y_j).
$$
For $a_i\in\{0,1\}$, let 
$\tau_i^{-1}(a_i)=\{x_i\in V(G_i):\tau_i(x_i)=a_i\}$ be the fiber of $\tau_i$ over $a_i$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:bridge-gate},
$\sum_{x_i\in\tau_i^{-1}(a_i)}\eta_i(x_i)=1$. 
Grouping the sum according
to $a=(\tau_1(x_1),\ldots,\tau_k(x_k))$ therefore gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{v\in V(G)}\Psi(v)
 &=\left(\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^k}\chi(a)
     \prod_{i=1}^k\sum_{x_i\in\tau_i^{-1}(a_i)}\eta_i(x_i)\right)
   \prod_{j=1}^{\ell}\sum_{y\in V(H_j)}\zeta_j(y)\\
 &=2\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}\sum_{y\in V(H_j)}\zeta_j(y)\ge2.
\end{align*}
Here each $\zeta_j$ has positive integral sum, and an empty product is one.
Thus the positive color class
$$
 U_+=\{v\in V(G):\Psi(v)=1\}
$$
has at least $N/2+1=\alpha(G)+1$ vertices.


It remains to bound its induced degree.  An edge in an $H_j$-direction
changes $\zeta_j$ and hence changes the sign of $\Psi$.  An edge in a $G_i$-direction other than the selected bridge
leaves $\tau_i$ unchanged and changes $\eta_i$, so it also changes the sign
of $\Psi$.  Across the selected bridge of $G_i$, the
$\eta_i$-value stays fixed while the $i$-th input of $\chi$ changes.  Such an
edge is monochromatic precisely when the corresponding cube edge is
monochromatic under $\chi$.  At a fixed product vertex these edges map to
distinct cube directions.  Lemma~\ref{lem:cube-coloring} therefore gives
$$
 \Delta(G[U_+])\le\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil.
$$
Delete vertices from $U_+$ if necessary until exactly $N/2+1$ remain.
Deletion does not increase maximum degree, so the lower and upper bounds
agree.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Every edge of a tree is a bridge.  Choose any edge from a perfect matching
of each $T_i$ and apply Theorem~\ref{thm:general-product} with no additional unbalanced factors.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:alpha-box}
If $n_1,\ldots,n_k\ge 2$ and $N=\prod_{i=1}^k n_i$, then
$$
 \alpha(P_{n_1}\square\cdots\square P_{n_k})=\left\lceil\frac{N}{2}\right\rceil.
$$
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $G=P_{n_1}\square\cdots\square P_{n_k}$.
Color a vertex $(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ by the parity of $x_1+\cdots+x_k$. The larger color class gives $\alpha(G)\ge\lceil N/2\rceil$.

To prove the reverse inequality, we construct a matching that
covers all but at most one vertex. For every fixed choice of
$x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}$, pair the vertices in the last coordinate
using the edges $(1,2),(3,4),(5,6),\ldots$.
If $n_k$ is even, this matches every vertex of $G$. If $n_k$
is odd, the unmatched vertices are precisely those with
$x_k=n_k$, and they induce a copy of
$P_{n_1}\square\cdots\square P_{n_{k-1}}$.
We then apply the same procedure to this remaining
$(k-1)$-dimensional product. Repeating recursively, we obtain a
matching $M$ that leaves at most one vertex unmatched. Thus
$|M|=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{2}\right\rfloor$.

An independent set contains at most one endpoint of each edge of
$M$, together with the possible unmatched vertex. Therefore,
$$
\alpha(G) \leq |M|+N-2|M|
=N-|M|
=\left\lceil\frac{N}{2}\right\rceil.
$$
The result follows.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:mixed-box}
Let $e\geq 1$ denote the number of even integers among
$n_1,\ldots,n_k$. Then
$$
 f(P_{n_1}\square\cdots\square P_{n_k})
 =\lceil\sqrt e\rceil.
$$
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Every even path has a perfect matching, every edge of a path is a bridge, and every odd path is unbalanced.  Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:general-product}, taking the $e$ even paths as the $G_i$ and the odd paths as the $H_j$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:odd-large}
Suppose that every $n_i$ is odd and at least one $n_i$ is at least $5$.
Then
$$
 f(P_{n_1}\square\cdots\square P_{n_k})=1.
$$
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Put $G=P_{n_1}\square\cdots\square P_{n_k}$ and $N=|V(G)|$.
Write $n_1=2t+1\ge5$ after reordering the factors. We assign signs to the vertices of the first path $P_{n_1}$ in their order along the path, namely
\begin{equation}
 ++-++(-+)^{t-2},
 \label{eq:sign-word}
\end{equation}
where $(-+)^{t-2}$ means $t-2$ repetitions of the pair $-+$.
Its sign sum is $3$, and each monochromatic component has at most two
vertices.  On every other odd path use its alternating bipartition character,
whose sign sum has absolute value $1$.  Color the product by the product of
these coordinate signs.  The total sign sum has absolute value $3$, so the
larger color class has
$$
 (N+3)/2=\alpha(G)+1
$$
vertices by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-box}.  Monochromatic edges can occur only in
the first coordinate, and the sign word \eqref{eq:sign-word} gives induced
maximum degree at most $1$.  Since a set of $\alpha(G)+1$ vertices cannot be
independent, equality follows.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:p3}
For every $k\ge 1$, $f(P_3^{\square k})=2$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of $P_3$ and put
$S=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1)$.  Then $SA=-AS$.  Define the signed adjacency matrix of $P_3^{\square k}$ by 
$$
 M_k=\sum_{i=1}^k
 S^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes A\otimes I_3^{\otimes(k-i)}.
 $$
The summands anticommute pairwise, so all cross terms vanish
when $M_k$ is squared. Thus, 
$$
 M_k^2=\sum_{i=1}^k
 I_3^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes A^2\otimes I_3^{\otimes(k-i)}.
$$
The eigenvalues of $A^2$ are $0,2,2$.  It follows that $M_k$ has a
one-dimensional kernel and that every nonzero eigenvalue has absolute value
at least $\sqrt 2$.  In addition, $M_k$ anticommutes with $S^{\otimes k}$. If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $M_k$ with eigenvector $\xi$, then $-\lambda$ is also an eigenvalue of $M_k$ with eigenvector $S^{\otimes k}\xi$. 
All nonzero eigenvalues of $M_k$ therefore occur in opposite pairs, and it has exactly
$(3^k-1)/2$ positive eigenvalues, all at least $\sqrt 2$.

Let $U\subseteq V(P_3^{\square k})$ have
$$
 |U|=\alpha(P_3^{\square k})+1=(3^k+3)/2.
$$
Ordering the eigenvalues of $M_k$ decreasingly, Cauchy interlacing yields
$$
 \lambda_{\max}(M_k[U])
 \ge\lambda_{(3^k-1)/2}(M_k)\ge\sqrt2.
$$
Since $M_k[U]$ is a signed adjacency matrix supported on
$P_3^{\square k}[U]$, its largest eigenvalue is at most its spectral radius, which is at most the maximum absolute row sum.  
The maximum absolute row sum of $M_k[U]$ equals $\Delta(P_3^{\square k}[U])$. Hence
$\Delta(P_3^{\square k}[U])\ge2$.

For the reverse inequality, give one $P_3$ factor the constant sign word
$+++$ and every other factor an alternating sign word.  The product coloring
has total sign sum of absolute value $3$, so its larger class has
$(3^k+3)/2$ vertices.  Its monochromatic edges occur only in the first
coordinate and have maximum degree $2$.  Hence $f(P_3^{\square k})\le 2$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:matching-cut-ft}
Let $k\ge1$, and let $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ be connected bipartite
graphs with perfect matchings.  For each $i$, fix a bipartition character
$\rho_i:V(B_i)\to\{-1,1\}$ and a map
$\tau_i:V(B_i)\to\{0,1\}$ whose $\tau_i$-cut is a matching.  Put
$$
 \gamma_i=\left|\sum_{\tau_i(x)=0}\rho_i(x)\right|,
 \quad \Gamma=\prod_{i=1}^k\gamma_i.
$$
If every $\gamma_i$ is positive, then, for $1\le t\le\Gamma$,
$$
 f_t(B_1\square\cdots\square B_k)=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil.
$$
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Set $G=B_1\square\cdots\square B_k$, $N=|V(G)|$, and
$D=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$.  The product is bipartite and has a perfect
matching, so $\alpha(G)=N/2$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:cube-cell-bound} gives
the required lower bound $f_t(G)\ge D$.

If $|V(B_i)|=2n_i$, then $\gamma_i\le n_i$, which implies 
$\Gamma\le\prod_i n_i\le N/2$. Hence every value of $t$ in the statement is in the domain of $f_t$.

After reversing $\rho_i$ when necessary, assume that
$\sum_{\tau_i=0}\rho_i=\gamma_i$.  Balance gives
$\sum_{\tau_i=1}\rho_i=-\gamma_i$.  Define
$$
 \eta_i(x)=(-1)^{\tau_i(x)}\rho_i(x).
$$
Thus the $\eta_i$-sum on either $\tau_i$-fiber is $\gamma_i$.  Let
$\chi:\{0,1\}^k\to\{-1,1\}$ be the coloring from
Lemma~\ref{lem:cube-coloring}.  On $G$ put
$$
 \Psi(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
 =\chi(\tau_1(x_1),\ldots,\tau_k(x_k))
   \prod_{i=1}^k\eta_i(x_i).
$$
The sum factorizes and equals
$$
 \sum_{x\in V(G)}\Psi(x)
 =\Gamma\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^k}\chi(a)=2\Gamma.
$$
Consequently the positive class has $N/2+\Gamma$ vertices.

Consider an edge in the $i$-th factor direction.  Off the $\tau_i$-cut, $\tau_i$ is unchanged and $\eta_i$ changes sign, so $\Psi$ changes sign. Across the cut, both $\tau_i$ and $\rho_i$ change, hence $\eta_i$ is unchanged; such an edge is monochromatic precisely when the corresponding
edge of $Q_k$ is monochromatic under $\chi$.  Since the cut is a matching, at a vertex $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$ there is at most one cut edge in each factor direction. Each monochromatic incident edge corresponds to a distinct monochromatic edge at $(\tau_1(x_1),\ldots,\tau_k(x_k))$ in $Q_k$. Hence there are at most $D$ such edges.
Delete $\Gamma-t$ positive vertices.  Passing to an induced subgraph cannot increase maximum degree, so this produces a set of order $N/2+t$ and induced maximum degree at most $D$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:path-gamma}
Let $r\ge1$, let $P_{2r}=v_1\cdots v_{2r}$, and put
$\rho(v_i)=(-1)^{i+1}$.  Among all maps
$\tau:V(P_{2r})\to\{0,1\}$ whose $\tau$-cut is a matching,
$$
 \max_\tau\left|\sum_{\tau(v)=0}\rho(v)\right|
 =\left\lceil\frac r3\right\rceil.
$$
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Fix an admissible map $\tau$, and set
$a_j=\tau(v_{2j})-\tau(v_{2j-1})$. Then
$$
\sum_{\tau(v)=0}\rho(v)=\sum_{j=1}^r a_j.
$$
If $a_j$ and $a_{j+1}$ are nonzero, the intervening edge
$v_{2j}v_{2j+1}$ is not in the $\tau$-cut, so
$a_{j+1}=-a_j$. Likewise, if $a_j,a_{j+2}\ne0$ and
$a_{j+1}=0$, the three intervening edges are not in the
cut, giving $a_{j+2}=-a_j$. Thus two consecutive nonzero terms whose indices differ by one or two have opposite signs. In particular, the nonzero terms within any three consecutive positions alternate, so their sum has absolute value at most one. Partitioning $[r]$ into consecutive blocks of
at most three indices yields
$$
\left|\sum_{j=1}^r a_j\right|
   \le \left\lceil\frac r3\right\rceil.
$$

For equality, let $\tau(v_1)=0$ and change its value
precisely across the edges $v_sv_{s+1}$ with
$s\equiv1\pmod 3$. These edges form a matching, and the
resulting sequence satisfies $a_j=1$ for
$j\equiv1\pmod 3$ and $a_j=0$ otherwise. Hence
$\sum_{j=1}^r a_j=\lceil r/3\rceil$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:path-ft-range}
Let $k\ge1 $ and $r_1,\ldots,r_k\ge1$, and set
$\Gamma=\prod_{i=1}^k\left\lceil\frac{r_i}{3}\right\rceil$.
Then for $1\le t\le\Gamma$
$$
 f_t(P_{2r_1}\square\cdots\square P_{2r_k})
 =\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil.
$$
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:separated-blocks}
Let $D,q\ge1$ be integers, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_q$ be bipartite graphs
with bipartition characters
$\rho_j$ satisfying $\sum_{x\in V(X_j)}\rho_j(x)=0$.
For each $j$, let $Z_j\subseteq V(X_j)$ be a nonempty set on which
$\rho_j$ is constant.  Suppose that distinct vertices of $Z_j$ are
at distance at least three in $X_j$, and that every vertex of $Z_j$
has degree at most $D$ in $X_j$.  If $q\le D$, then
$X=X_1\square\cdots\square X_q$ has a coloring
$\sigma:V(X)\to\{-1,1\}$ with
$$
 \left|\sum_{x\in V(X)}\sigma(x)\right|
 =2\prod_{j=1}^q|Z_j|
$$
and monochromatic degree at most $D$ at every vertex.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let $b_j$ be zero on $Z_j$ and one elsewhere, and set
$$
 F(x)=\prod_{j=1}^q b_j(x_j),\quad
 \rho(x)=\prod_{j=1}^q\rho_j(x_j),\quad
 \sigma(x)=\rho(x)(-1)^{F(x)}.
$$
Since each block is balanced and $\rho_j$ is constant on $Z_j$,
$$
 \left|\sum_{x\in V(X_j)}\rho_j(x)b_j(x)\right|=|Z_j|.
$$
The sums factor over the blocks.  Using $(-1)^{F(x)}=1-2F(x)$ and
$\sum_x\rho(x)=0$, we obtain
$$
 \left|\sum_x\sigma(x)\right|
 =2\left|\sum_x\rho(x)F(x)\right|
 =2\prod_{j=1}^q|Z_j|.
$$

Across every edge, $\rho$ changes sign.  Thus an edge is
monochromatic under $\sigma$ exactly when $F$ changes.
If at least two block values are zero, changing one coordinate
cannot change $F$.  If exactly one block value is zero, only
edges leaving that block's zero set can change $F$, and there
are at most $D$ such edges.  If no block value is zero, each
block contributes at most one edge on which $F$ changes:
a vertex adjacent to two distinct points of $Z_j$ would put
those points at distance at most two.  The total is therefore
at most $q\le D$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:pm-tree-leaves}
Let $T$ be a tree with a perfect matching and bipartition $(X,Y)$.  Then each
of $X$ and $Y$ contains a leaf.  Moreover, if $T\ne K_2$, then any two
distinct leaves of $T$ are at distance at least three.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Write $|X|=|Y|=n$.  If, say, $X$ contained no leaf, then every vertex of $X$ would have degree at least two. Thus
$$
 |E(T)|=\sum_{v\in X}d(v)\ge 2n,
$$
contrary to $|E(T)|=2n-1$.  The argument for $Y$ is the same.  Two leaves can be adjacent only when the connected tree is $K_2$.  Two leaves at distance two have a common neighbor, but then both incident leaf edges would be forced into every perfect matching, which is impossible.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:even-code}
For every integer $D\ge1$, put $m=\lceil\log_2D\rceil$.
There is a set $\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^D$ of at least
$2^{D-m-1}$ even-weight words such that distinct words have
Hamming distance at least four.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Choose distinct vectors $h_1,\ldots,h_D\in\mathbb F_2^m$ and set
$$
 \mathcal C=\left\{c\in\mathbb F_2^D:
 \sum_{i=1}^D c_i=0,\quad
 \sum_{i=1}^D c_i h_i=0\right\}.
$$
These are at most $m+1$ linear constraints, so
$|\mathcal C|\ge2^{D-m-1}$.  Every word has even weight.
A word of weight two would imply $h_i=h_j$ for two distinct
indices, which is impossible.  Since $\mathcal C$ is a linear space,
the difference of two distinct words has weight at least four.
For $D=1$, take $\mathbb F_2^0=\{0\}$; the construction gives
$\mathcal C=\{0\}$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $G=T_1\square\cdots\square T_k$, 
$m=\lceil\log_2D\rceil$ and $N=|V(G)|$.
Since $D=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil\le k$, the hypotheses imply
$t\le2^{D-1}\le2^{k-1}\le N/2$, so $f_t(G)$ is defined.
Moreover, $\alpha(G)=N/2$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:cube-cell-bound} gives $f_t(G)\ge D$.

Fix bipartition characters $\rho_i$ of the factors.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:pm-tree-leaves}, each $T_i$ has leaves
$a_i^0,a_i^1$ in opposite bipartition classes.
Since $D\le k\le D^2$, partition $[k]$ into nonempty blocks
$I_1,\ldots,I_q$ with
$$
 |I_1|=D,\quad |I_j|\le D\ (j\ge2),\quad q\le D.
$$
Such a partition exists because, after reserving $D$ indices,
the remaining at most $D(D-1)$ indices fit into at most
$D-1$ further blocks.  Write
$$
 X_j=\mathop{\square}_{i\in I_j}T_i,
 \quad \rho_{I_j}(x)=\prod_{i\in I_j}\rho_i(x_i).
$$
Each $X_j$ is balanced.

Identify $I_1$ with $[D]$, and choose $t$ words from the code
in Lemma~\ref{lem:even-code}.  For the chosen set $\mathcal C'$, put
$$
 Z_1=\{(a_i^{c_i})_{i\in I_1}:c\in\mathcal C'\}
 \subseteq V(X_1).
$$
The words have even weight, so $\rho_{I_1}$ is constant on $Z_1$.
The distance between two resulting tuples is at least the
Hamming distance between their words, and hence is at least four.
Every point of $Z_1$ has degree $D$, since all its coordinates
are leaves.  For $j\ge2$, let $Z_j$ consist of one all-leaf tuple
in $X_j$; its degree is $|I_j|\le D$.

Lemma~\ref{lem:separated-blocks} now gives a coloring of $G$
with imbalance $2t$ and monochromatic degree at most $D$.
Its larger class has $N/2+t=\alpha(G)+t$ vertices, proving
$f_t(G)\le D$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $G=T_1\square\cdots\square T_k$ and $N=|V(G)|$. Then $\alpha(G)=N/2$ and
Lemma~\ref{lem:cube-cell-bound} gives $f_2(G)\ge D$.

Fix bipartition characters $\rho_i$ and relabel the factors so
that $T_1\ne K_2$.  Since $2\le D\le k\le D^2$, choose a
partition $I_1,\ldots,I_q$ of $[k]$ with
$$
 q\le D,\quad |I_j|\le D,\quad
 |I_1|=D,\quad 1,2\in I_1.
$$
Write $X_j=\mathop{\square}_{i\in I_j}T_i$ and
$\rho_{I_j}=\prod_{i\in I_j}\rho_i$.

Take distinct leaves $u,v$ of $T_1$.  If
$\rho_1(u)=\rho_1(v)$, use the same fixed leaf in every other
coordinate of two tuples in $X_1$.  If
$\rho_1(u)=-\rho_1(v)$, choose leaves $w,w'$ of $T_2$ in opposite
bipartition classes and use $(u,w)$ and $(v,w')$ in the first two
coordinates; keep every remaining coordinate fixed at a leaf.
In either case we obtain all-leaf tuples $z_1,z'_1$ with
$$
 \rho_{I_1}(z_1)=\rho_{I_1}(z'_1),\quad
 d_{X_1}(z_1,z'_1)\ge4.
$$
Indeed, Lemma~\ref{lem:pm-tree-leaves} gives $d_{T_1}(u,v)\ge3$.
In the first case this distance is even and hence at least four;
in the second case the second coordinate contributes at least one
more to the product distance.

Set $Z_1=\{z_1,z'_1\}$, and for each $j\ge2$ let $Z_j$ consist
of one all-leaf tuple in $X_j$.  Every point of $Z_j$ has degree
$|I_j|\le D$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:separated-blocks} gives a coloring
with imbalance four and monochromatic degree at most $D$.
Its larger class has $N/2+2$ vertices, proving the upper bound.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:even-path-ftwo}
Let $k\ge2$ and $r_1,\ldots,r_k\ge1$.  If some $r_i\ge2$, then
$$
 f_2(P_{2r_1}\square\cdots\square P_{2r_k})
 =\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil.
$$
Thus the only product of at least two even paths not covered by this corollary
is the hypercube $P_2^{\square k}=Q_k$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:one-path-ftwo}
For $r\ge 2$,
$$
 f_2(P_{2r})=
 \begin{cases}
  2,& r=2,3,\\
  1,& r\ge 4.
 \end{cases}
$$
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The elementary path formula
$\operatorname{diss}(P_n)=\lceil2n/3\rceil$ follows by partitioning the path into consecutive triples, with a final block of one or two vertices:
a maximum-degree-one set contains at most two vertices from each triple, and the repeating word $110$ (where $1$ means selected) attains the bound including the remainder one or two vertices.
For $n=4,6$, $\operatorname{diss}(P_n)=\lceil2n/3\rceil < n/2+2=\alpha(P_n)+2$, so $f_2(P_n)\ge2$; the reverse inequality follows from
$\Delta(P_n)=2$.  If $n=2r$ with $r\ge4$, then
$$
 \operatorname{diss}(P_{2r})=\left\lceil\frac{4r}{3}\right\rceil
 \ge r+2=\alpha(P_{2r})+2,
$$
so a maximum dissociation set contains a subset of exactly
$r+2=\alpha(P_{2r})+2$ vertices and $f_2(P_{2r})\le1$. A set of more than $\alpha(P_{2r})$ vertices cannot be independent.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:cube-excess-two-large}
$f_2(Q_n)=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil$ for $n\ge 10$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
For $n\ge 10$, $D=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil\ge 4$ and $2^{D-\lceil\log_2 D\rceil-1}\ge 2$. Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:fixed-excess-intro} (i) with every factor equal to $K_2$ gives the upper bound, and Huang's theorem gives the lower bound.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:cube-excess-two-small}
For $n\in\{2,3,5,6,7,8\}$,
$f_2(Q_n)=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil$.
In contrast, $f_2(Q_4)=3$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Huang's theorem gives the required lower bounds for $n \neq 4$. For $Q_2$, take the whole cube.  For $Q_3$, delete an antipodal pair; the remaining six vertices induce a cycle.

We use Lemma~\ref{lem:parity-twist-excess} for the other upper bounds.
Define $F_5:\{0,1\}^5\to\{0,1\}$ by declaring $F_5(x)=1$ when $|x|\le2$ or when
$$
\operatorname{supp}(x)\in\mathcal T=
 \bigl\{\{1,2,5\},\{1,3,4\},\{2,3,4\},\{3,4,5\}\bigr\}.
$$
The four triples in $\mathcal T$ cover every pair of $[5]$, and no
four-subset contains all four triples.  A zero of weight three has exactly three neighbors in the one-set; a zero of weight four has at most three selected triple neighbors; a zero of weight five has no neighbors in the one-set.  At a vertex of weight two, $F_5=1$, and at most two of its three neighbors of weight three have value zero, since every pair is contained in a triple of $\mathcal T$. At a selected triple, only its two neighbors of weight four have value zero. Therefore
$$
s_0(F_5)\le3,\quad s_1(F_5)\le2,\quad A(F_5)=1-5+10-4=2.
$$
This settles $n=5$.

Define $g_3:\{0,1\}^3\to\{0,1\}$ by setting $g_3(x)=1$ exactly when $|x|\le 1$. Then
$$
 s_0(g_3)=s_1(g_3)=2, \quad A(g_3)=1-3=-2.
$$
The Boolean $\operatorname{OR}_3$ function has alternating sum $A(\operatorname{OR}_3)=-1$ and $s_0(\operatorname{OR}_3)=3$, $s_1(\operatorname{OR}_3)=1$. Hence, the function
$$
 F_6=g_3\wedge\operatorname{OR}_3
$$
on two disjoint three-coordinate blocks has $A(F_6)=2$ and $s(F_6)\le 3$.  This settles $n=6$.

On four variables, fix $P\in\binom{[4]}2$ and define $g_4=0$ exactly on the vectors of weight at most one and on the vector with support $P$.
Then
$$
s_0(g_4)\le 3,\quad s_1(g_4)\le 2,\quad  A(g_4)=2.
$$
Indeed, a zero singleton outside $P$ has three one-neighbors, while all other zero cases have at most two; a one of weight two has at most its two lower zero-neighbors. Ones of weights three and four have sensitivity at most one and zero, respectively. It follows that
$$
 F_7=g_4\wedge\operatorname{OR}_3
 \text{ and }
 F_8=F_5\wedge\operatorname{OR}_3
$$
have $|A(F_7)|=|A(F_8)|=2$ and sensitivities at most
three. They settle $n=7,8$.

For the upper bound in $Q_4$, let $W=\{000,001,010,101,110\}\subseteq V(Q_3)$.
Then $|W|=5$ and $\Delta(Q_3[W])=2$, so
$W\times\{0,1\}\subseteq Q_4$ has ten vertices and induced maximum degree
three.

It remains to exclude induced maximum degree two.  Let $E,O$ be the two
parity classes of $Q_4$, let $U\subseteq V(Q_4)$ have size ten, and suppose
to the contrary that $\Delta(Q_4[U])\le2$.  Interchanging $E$ and $O$
if necessary, put
$$
 X=U\cap O,
 \quad a=|X|\le5,
 \quad Y=E\setminus U.
$$
Since $|U|=10$ and $|E|=8$, we have $|Y|=a-2$. Each vertex of $X$ has
at least two neighbors in $Y$, so
$$
 2a\le e(X,Y)\le 4(a-2), 
$$
which implies $a=4$ or $a=5$.

If $a=4$, equality holds throughout, so every vertex of $X$ is a common
neighbor of the two vertices of $Y$.  This is impossible: two distinct
vertices in one parity class of $Q_4$ have two common neighbors when their
distance is two and none when their distance is four.

If $a=5$, then $|Y|=3$ and at least five odd vertices have two or more neighbors in $Y$.  For $v\in O$, write $d_Y(v)=|N(v)\cap Y|$.  Counting pairs consisting of an odd vertex and two of its neighbors in $Y$ gives
$$
 \sum_{v\in O}\binom{d_Y(v)}2
 =\sum_{\{y,y'\}\in\binom Y 2}|N(y)\cap N(y')|.
$$
At least five vertices of $X$ contribute one each, so the left-hand side is at least five. If $Y$ contains an antipodal pair, that pair contributes zero on the right, and each of the other two pairs contributes at most two, a contradiction.  Hence all three
pairs in $Y$ are at distance two. By translating one vertex of $Y$ to $0000$, the other two vertices have weight two and supports intersecting in exactly one coordinate. Permuting the coordinates, we may therefore assume that
$$
 Y=\{0000,1100,1010\}.
$$
The multiset $\{d_Y(v):v\in O\}$ is $\{3,2,2,2,1,1,1,0\}$,
and the odd vertices with at least two neighbors in $Y$ are
$1000,0100,0010,1110$.  Thus only four odd vertices have at least two
neighbors in $Y$, again a contradiction. Therefore $f_2(Q_4)=3$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
\label{prob:matched-factors}
Characterize the connected bipartite graphs $B$ with perfect matchings such
that
$$
 f(B^{\square k})=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil
 \qquad\text{for every }k\ge1.
$$
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:one-sided-versus-two-sided}
Let $G$ have bipartition $\{u,a,b,c\}\sqcup\{v,x,y,z\}$ and edge set
$$
 E(G)=\{uv,ux,uy,uz,va,vb,vc,ax,ay,by,cz\}.
$$
Then $f(G)=1$ but $\iota_1(G)=0$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The edges $uv,ax,by,cz$ form a perfect matching, so $\alpha(G)=4$.
The set $\{a,b,c,x,z\}$ induces two independent edges and an isolated
vertex, giving $f(G)=1$.
A set of five vertices inducing maximum degree at most one cannot contain
$u$: it would have to contain all of $a,b,c$ and exactly one neighbor of
$u$, each choice producing a vertex of degree at least two.
The same argument excludes $v$.
The remaining six vertices induce the path $xayb$ and the edge $cz$.
Thus the only possible five-vertex sets are
$\{a,b,c,x,z\}$ and $\{b,c,x,y,z\}$, whose complements both induce $P_3$.
There is no larger set inducing maximum degree at most one.
Consequently no such two-sided coloring has unequal class sizes, whereas
the bipartition itself gives imbalance zero.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- problem-2: body_md -->
\label{prob:excess}
Determine whether $f_2(Q_9)=3$ or $4$.  More generally, sharpen the factor threshold in Theorem~\ref{thm:fixed-excess-intro} (i), and determine $f_t$ in the remaining finite-factor cases for hypercubes, Cartesian products of trees with perfect matchings, and Cartesian products of even-order paths.
